issues.legal_issue: An appellate court may reverse an acquittal when the trial court’s assessment of credible evidence is perverse and no other reasonable view is available.
material_facts: The prosecution presented two eyewitnesses whose accounts described the origin and manner of the assault, and other witnesses substantially corroborated their account.
The trial court rejected evidence on trivial discrepancies, speculative grounds, and a misreading of the testimony.
The Supreme Court found the trial court’s conclusions unsustainable and noted that the High Court considered whether any other view was reasonably possible.
issues.conclusion: The reversal of the acquittal and the resulting convictions were upheld; the appeals and special leave petition were dismissed.
issues.legal_principle: An appellate court can reverse an acquittal where the trial court’s findings are perverse, based on a misreading of evidence or speculation, and the evidence supports no other reasonably possible view. The Court referred generally to principles previously laid down by it concerning reversal of acquittals but identified no earlier case by name. The convictions affirmed were under Sections 302/34 and 302/114 of the Indian Penal Code.

rule.if: appeal_from_acquittal and credible_eyewitness_account and (trial_court_misread_evidence or trial_court_relied_on_trivial_discrepancies_or_speculation) and no_other_reasonable_view

predicates.appeal_from_acquittal: The proceeding is an appeal from a judgment acquitting the accused.
predicates.credible_eyewitness_account: Witnesses who observed the occurrence gave a reliable account of how it began and unfolded.
predicates.trial_court_misread_evidence: The trial court misunderstood or misread material testimony.
predicates.trial_court_relied_on_trivial_discrepanc: The trial court rejected evidence on minor inconsistencies or speculative grounds.
predicates.no_other_reasonable_view: The evidence does not reasonably support a view other than the one adopted by the appellate court.

issues.definition: When an appeal challenges an acquittal, reliable eyewitness evidence, an unsound trial-court assessment, and the absence of another reasonable view support upholding the reversal and resulting convictions.

issues.legal_issue: The nonproduction of an alleged initial report does not by itself undermine the prosecution where the accused were promptly identified and the report was lodged soon after the occurrence.
material_facts: A witness disclosed the accused persons’ names to other witnesses soon after the occurrence.
The formal report was lodged within an hour or two of the occurrence.
A report bearing the complainant’s signature was not produced, and the defence argued that it concealed an earlier report omitting some accused persons.
The Court found no evidentiary basis for the alleged concealment and noted that the injured accused persons’ participation was explained by the eyewitnesses.
issues.conclusion: The alleged nonproduction of the report did not detract from the prosecution case.
issues.legal_principle: The Court treated the suggested concealment of an earlier report as speculation in light of the prompt disclosure of the accused persons’ identities and the prompt lodging of the formal report. It cited no provision or earlier case for this evidentiary conclusion.

rule.if: criminal_prosecution and prompt_identification_of_accused and prompt_formal_report and alleged_initial_report_not_produced and no_evidence_of_concealment

predicates.criminal_prosecution: The proceeding is a criminal prosecution in which the timing and contents of reports about the offence are disputed.
predicates.prompt_identification_of_accused: Witnesses identified the accused to others soon after the occurrence.
predicates.prompt_formal_report: A formal report was lodged soon after the occurrence.
predicates.alleged_initial_report_not_produced: A report said to have been prepared or signed earlier was not produced in court.
predicates.no_evidence_of_concealment: The evidence does not establish that the prosecution deliberately withheld a report to conceal information.

issues.definition: In a criminal prosecution, prompt identification and reporting, together with the absence of evidence of deliberate concealment, mean that nonproduction of an alleged initial report does not undermine the prosecution.

issues.legal_issue: A claim of private defence is unavailable where the accused continue a fatal assault after the victims have fallen and are incapable of resistance.
material_facts: The accused and the deceased parties had a chronic land dispute, and a prior threat to kill had been reported.
The accused inflicted numerous injuries on three victims, who died from their injuries.
Eyewitnesses testified that the accused continued assaulting two victims after they had fallen and were harmless and unable to resist.
The Court found that the nature and manner of the attack did not support a justification of private defence.
issues.conclusion: The private-defence claim was rejected, and the murder convictions were upheld.
issues.legal_principle: The Court applied Exception 2 to Section 300 of the Indian Penal Code in considering the claim that the accused had exceeded a right of private defence. It concluded on the evidence that the claim could not be accepted, particularly because the assault continued after the victims were incapacitated. No earlier case was identified for this conclusion.

predicates.homicide_prosecution: The proceeding concerns a prosecution for causing deaths.
predicates.repeated_fatal_assault: The accused inflicted numerous injuries in an assault that caused the victims’ deaths.
predicates.assault_continued_after_victims_incapaci: The assailants continued attacking victims after they had fallen and could no longer resist.

issues.definition: In a homicide prosecution, repeated fatal violence that continues after the victims are incapacitated means the claim of private defence is rejected and the murder conviction is sustained.
